name: Firmus
ownership: Private (backed by NVIDIA, Coatue and Blackstone)
snippet: Australian builder and operator of liquid-cooled NVIDIA AI factories across Asia-Pacific. It has more than 900 MW contracted, with Meta and OpenAI as anchors, and withdrew its ASX IPO in October 2026.
origin: Firmus started in 2019 in Tasmania, where it ran bitcoin mining and high-performance computing on hydro power using its own immersion cooling. It finished early HyperCube research in 2020 and a renewable-powered immersion-cooled data hall in 2021. In 2023 it launched Sustainable Metal Cloud, a bare-metal GPU service built with ST Telemedia Global Data Centres and first offered in Singapore. Co-founder Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis lead the company as co-CEOs.
today: Firmus raised $505M in a Coatue-led round at a $5.5B valuation in April 2026, then $2B from Coatue, NVIDIA, Blackstone funds and Jane Street at a post-money valuation above $10.5B in August 2026. Blackstone led a $10B debt facility with Coatue support in February 2026 for Project Southgate, which targets up to 1.6 GW of AI capacity across Australian states by 2028. Southgate's Melbourne site hosts about 18,400 GB300 GPUs under a multi-year hyperscaler contract, and Meta is the anchor customer there. A Tasmanian Southgate campus with about 36,800 GB300 GPUs is due in late 2026. In June 2026 Firmus and NVIDIA announced a 360 MW campus in Batam, Indonesia, for up to 170,000 NVIDIA accelerators, with $25B to $30B of expected committed offtake over six years. OpenAI became an anchor customer at two Malaysian sites in September 2026, which lifted contracted capacity above 900 MW, and Meta added capacity in Southeast Asia later that month. CDC Data Centres ended its Southgate partnership on October 6, 2026 after about 42 MW, and Firmus withdrew its planned ASX IPO, which sought about A$7B at an A$44B valuation, three days later.
platform: Firmus builds its sites from HyperCube, a prefabricated unit that combines liquid cooling, mechanical systems and electrification, which the company manufactures in regional New South Wales. Its AI factories follow the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture and host GB300 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 racks with Spectrum-X networking. Firmus AI Cloud sells bare metal, cloud compute and storage on this infrastructure. Fireworks AI signed a multi-year deal in August 2026 to run on its Asia-based cloud region.
outlook: Firmus says it will pursue private funding after pulling the IPO. ABC News reported that investors questioned the valuation, debt projected at about $30B by 2028, and the fact that only two of its seven sites operate. ABC also cited investor concern about co-CEO Oliver Curtis's past insider trading conviction. The company targets the five sites under development within 24 months, the Tasmanian campus in late 2026 and first Batam capacity in the first quarter of 2027.

editor_notes: HQ set to Sydney because Firmus press releases give Sydney. Mingtiandi lists Tasmania, where the company started, and techpartner.news called it Tasmania-based in 2023. Seed facts confirmed, including $2B at above $10.5B (August 2026), $505M at $5.5B (April 2026), the $10B Southgate debt (February 2026), 900+ MW contracted, OpenAI at two Malaysian sites, and 18,400 plus 36,800 GB300 GPUs. The March 2026 Melbourne contract named no customer. The later Firmus Meta release and W.Media place Meta at Melbourne on GB300 NVL72, so the profile treats Meta as the Melbourne anchor without stating that the 18,400 GPUs are all Meta's. New since the seed are the end of the CDC partnership (October 6, 2026) and the IPO withdrawal (October 9, 2026). The bitcoin mining origin rests on a Forbes headline (article not fetched) and secondary profiles. A secondary source names a third co-founder, Jonathan Levee, which I could not verify, so the profile omits him. Category is neocloud because Firmus owns GPUs and sells capacity, though it also develops its own sites. ABC reported NVIDIA holds about 7.2%.

name: GMI Cloud
snippet: Mountain View GPU cloud with close ties to Taiwan's AI supply chain and a GB300 AI factory in Taiwan. It raised $668M in equity and credit in September 2026 and reports over $600M in contracted ARR.
origin: Alex Yeh founded GMI Cloud in 2021, and press accounts say he turned an earlier Bitcoin mining business in Taiwan into a GPU cloud after China's 2021 crypto ban. The company grew around Taiwan's AI hardware chain, with Wistron as a customer and Compal, Macnica and Taiwan Mobile as partners. It raised an $82M Series A of equity and debt led by Headline Asia in October 2024.
today: GMI Cloud announced $668M on September 30, 2026, made up of a $223M Series B led by ARCHIV with NVIDIA participating and a $445M credit facility led by CTBC. KB Investment, Kyobo Life, KT, DSC Investment and Trend Micro joined the equity round. The company reports contracted ARR above $600M, more than nine times its end-2025 level, and about 4 trillion inference tokens a week. Its $500M Taiwan AI factory, with about 7,000 GB300 GPUs in 96 racks drawing 16 MW, began operating in March 2026. That same month GMI announced a 1 GW, $12B sovereign AI campus on Vera Rubin NVL72 in Satsumasendai, Kagoshima, Japan, with a first 200 MW phase planned for 2028. In July 2026 GMI committed $500M of capital spending backed by nine-figure contracts with a leading US frontier AI company. NVIDIA recognized it as an Exemplar Cloud for GB300 NVL72 training in August 2026.
platform: GMI sells dedicated bare-metal H100, H200 and Blackwell GPUs, a Cluster Engine for multi-node orchestration and a serverless Inference Engine that scales to zero. Agentbox, launched in June 2026, bundles execution sandboxes, inference, observability and distribution for AI agents, and GMI Router picks a model for each prompt. The company reports more than 30,000 GPUs deployed. Reuters reported in November 2025 that GMI runs data centers in the United States, Taiwan, Singapore, Thailand and Japan.
outlook: Reuters reported in November 2025 that GMI was developing a 50 MW US data center and planned an IPO within 2 to 3 years. GMI plans to start building the Kagoshima campus in late 2026 with partners including Kai Shin Digital Infrastructure, CDIB Capital and the Kagoshima prefectural government. The company says it will spend the new funds on capacity in the US, Taiwan and Asia-Pacific and on its inference services.

editor_notes: Founding year set to 2021 per Pulse 2.0 and Progressive Robot, which contradicts the seed's 2023. The Bitcoin mining origin and the $82M Series A come only from Progressive Robot, which cites WOWTALE. I could not verify the seed's DCD detail that the company first served Bitcoin mining data centers. I could not verify the seed's Vantage Taipei location for the Taiwan AI factory. BigGo Finance says the factory was converted from Taiwan Mobile's Taoyuan data center, so the profile gives no city. I could not verify the seed's $635M contract-backed loan for a 25 MW Taoyuan facility with Taiwan Mobile (BTW Media), so the profile omits it. The March 2026 opening date for the Taiwan factory comes from BigGo Finance. The 50 MW US site and IPO timing come from Reuters in November 2025 and may be stale. The 200 MW first Japan phase in 2028 comes from GMI's July 2026 release. Region is North America by HQ, but most capacity, partners and investors are in Asia, mainly Taiwan, Japan and Korea. Reflection AI is listed as a customer based on GMI's November 2025 partnership announcement. Search budget ran out before the Agentbox and Exemplar items could be cross-checked in press, so those rest on GMI's own posts.

name: Megaspeed
snippet: Singapore GPU cloud and NVIDIA Cloud Partner. US and Singapore authorities opened investigations in 2025 into reported diversion of Nvidia chips to China, and the company says inspections found no violations.
origin: Implicator.ai reported in October 2025 that Megaspeed was carved out of 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud company with state-backed investors. Bloomberg reported in December 2025 that the company is said to have spun off from 7Road. Megaspeed describes itself as a specialized GPU cloud and an NVIDIA Cloud Partner in Asia-Pacific. It lists an office at Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore and an Indonesian entity, PT Megaspeed International Indonesia, with an office in Jakarta.
today: The New York Times reported in October 2025 that US Commerce Department officials were investigating whether Megaspeed was helping companies in China sidestep US export controls, and that it was positioned to buy about $2B of Nvidia technology over the following year. Singapore police said they were investigating the company for potential breaches of local law, according to Implicator.ai. In December 2025 Bloomberg reported a wider US probe and said Malaysian and Indonesian customs records showed Megaspeed importing at least $4.6B of Nvidia hardware, or more than 136,000 GPUs. Bloomberg also reported that an Nvidia inspection found only a few thousand Blackwell chips at Megaspeed's data centers and that Nvidia confirmed more inventory at separate warehouses, according to a summary by The Economy. Nvidia said in October 2025 that it had no evidence Megaspeed diverted chips to China and that its checks found no Chinese shareholders, as reported by Implicator.ai. Megaspeed said in a December 2025 statement that inspections by the US Bureau of Industry and Security, Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry and NVIDIA found no evidence of violations, and that it reserves the right to take legal action.
platform: Megaspeed's website lists GPU compute on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and HGX H100 systems, along with CPU instances, managed Kubernetes, virtual servers, distributed storage and an inference service. It describes two data centers in Asia and direct-to-chip liquid cooling for its GB200 deployments.
outlook: The Singapore and US investigations reported in 2025 are the main item to watch. Implicator.ai reported that Megaspeed's Nvidia orders stopped by late July 2025, the same month Malaysia tightened permits for Nvidia chip exports and transfers.

editor_notes: The New York Times and Bloomberg originals are paywalled, so allegation details come from secondary summaries (Implicator.ai, The Fly via TipRanks, The Economy) and should be checked against the originals before publishing. I verified no 2026 developments because the search budget ran out before I could check 2026 coverage, so the profile does not know whether the investigations produced charges, penalties or closure by October 2026. Founding year is blank. Search snippets of the 2025 coverage give 2023, but no fetched page confirmed it. Reporting names Huang Le (Alice Huang) as founder or former executive and says Singapore police questioned her, and The Economy cites reports that Megaspeed leased chips to Alibaba. The profile omits both because the sourcing is secondhand and one concerns a private individual. Implicator.ai also says trade records show most orders flowed through Aivres, the US arm of Inspur, without naming its source, so the profile omits that claim too. The website gives the Singapore address and an Indonesian operating entity, and Bloomberg's customs data came from Malaysia and Indonesia. No named customers have public evidence.
